clinicalPearls: Scleromalacia perforans is a form of anterior necrotising scleritis occurring characteristically WITHOUT inflammation and WITHOUT pain, which is why it is so easily overlooked despite being sight- and globe-threatening.
It is strongly associated with long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, typically in older women with severe deforming disease, and is regarded as a marker of systemic vasculitic activity.

The hallmark is progressive scleral thinning with the appearance of yellow-grey necrotic plaques and increasingly visible bluish underlying uvea; despite the name, actual perforation is uncommon unless trauma or raised intraocular pressure supervenes.
Because it is painless and quiet, patients may present late with an incidental blue-grey patch or with astigmatic visual change rather than with a red painful eye.

Management is fundamentally systemic: aggressive immunosuppression, frequently with corticosteroids plus a steroid-sparing agent or a biologic, in close liaison with rheumatology, because the eye disease reflects underlying systemic vasculitis with excess mortality.
Topical therapy is largely supportive; ocular lubrication and protection are used but do not alter the necrotising process.
Surgery is avoided where possible because the necrotic sclera heals poorly; scleral or tectonic patch grafting is reserved for impending or actual perforation.

New-onset necrotising scleritis mandates a work-up for systemic vasculitis and exclusion of infection, as an underlying connective-tissue or ANCA-associated disorder frequently coexists and dictates prognosis.
reference.pathophysiology: The lesion is driven by immune-complex-mediated occlusive microvasculitis of the deep episcleral and scleral vessels, most often in the setting of long-standing rheumatoid arthritis. Vascular occlusion produces ischaemia of the avascular scleral collagen, and infiltrating macrophages and matrix metalloproteinases degrade the scleral matrix, causing progressive necrosis and thinning. Uniquely, the classic cellular inflammatory response is muted or absent, so the eye remains white and painless while the sclera melts away, exposing the underlying dark uvea. Continued matrix breakdown risks staphylomatous ectasia and, rarely, perforation.
additionalDifferentials: Infective (e.g. pseudomonal or fungal) scleritis and surgically induced necrotising scleritis
Scleral thinning from prior surgery or trauma
Choroidal or ciliary body melanoma showing through thin sclera
Blue sclera of osteogenesis imperfecta or other collagen disorders
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination with red-free light to map scleral thinning and avascular necrotic areas
Rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP antibodies and inflammatory markers
ANCA, antinuclear antibody and complement to screen for systemic vasculitis
Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography or high-frequency ultrasound to quantify residual scleral thickness
Screening for infection when a necrotising process could be microbial, including scrape and culture
Systemic vasculitis and infection screen (chest imaging, urinalysis, renal function) in liaison with rheumatology
redFlags: Rapidly progressive scleral thinning with staphyloma formation or impending perforation
Exposure of uvea through frankly necrotic sclera
Systemic features of active vasculitis (renal, pulmonary or neurological involvement)
Signs suggesting infective scleritis, which mimics and requires urgent culture-directed antimicrobials
Any globe rupture following minor trauma to markedly thinned sclera
reference.prognosis: Ocular prognosis is guarded and depends on early control of the underlying systemic disease; untreated it can progress to staphyloma or perforation. Its appearance signals severe systemic vasculitis and is associated with increased mortality, so outcome is tied to systemic rather than purely ocular management.
pitfalls: Dismissing a white, painless eye as benign and missing sight-threatening necrotising scleritis
Treating the eye in isolation without instituting or escalating systemic immunosuppression
Failing to exclude infective scleritis before committing to immunosuppression
Undertaking scleral surgery on actively necrotic tissue, precipitating further melt (surgically induced necrotising scleritis)
Overlooking the associated excess systemic mortality and not co-managing with rheumatology

Treat the underlying rheumatoid disease in close liaison with rheumatology, since the eye reflects systemic vasculitic activity
Provide supportive ocular care with lubricants and eye protection, recognising topical therapy does not halt the necrotising process
Protect the thinned globe from trauma and raised intraocular pressure, and consider scleral or tectonic patch grafting for impending perforation
Monitor residual scleral thickness and screen for systemic vasculitis and the associated excess mortality
Coordinate multidisciplinary rheumatology and ophthalmology follow-up, addressing cardiovascular and systemic risk
